title: American soft power
subtitle: Attraction, not conquest
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: How can a country dominate the world without going to war? By simply making others want to look like it.

hero.hook: Charming the world instead of conquering it: the secret of American power.

blocks.text: How can a country dominate the world without going to war? By simply making others want to look like it. That is the idea behind **soft power**, the art of attracting rather than forcing, a concept that changed the way we understand relations between countries.
The United States is the most studied example of it. But this influence through attraction, powerful as it is, now shows signs of fragility.

In 1990, in his book *Bound to Lead*, the American political scientist **Joseph Nye** coined a new term: **soft power**. He set it against **hard power**, the blunt kind, made of armies and economic sanctions. Soft power rests on attraction: convincing rather than forcing. For Nye it stands on three pillars: **culture**, when other peoples enjoy it, **political values** such as democracy, so long as they are truly applied at home, and **foreign policy**, which is legitimate when the rest of the world sees it as fair.

Hollywood makes about 700 films a year, against more than 1,800 for Bollywood in India. Yet American films take in roughly 70% of world cinema revenue: proof that reach depends less on quantity than on control of the distribution networks.

This ability to win others over without forcing them recalls an older idea, **[[Cultural hegemony]]**: dominating not by force, but by making your own ideas look like obvious truths that everyone shares.

Since the end of the First World War, the United States has built a cultural empire with no equal. American cinema exports a way of life, consumer habits and the English language. Music, from jazz to hip-hop, extends that influence, and so do the elite universities of the **[[Ivy League]]**, which train a good share of the world's leaders.

blocks.caption: For a century, Hollywood, music and American universities have exported a way of life admired around the world

blocks.text: In the 21st century that power has moved to the digital world. American technology giants control the search algorithms and the social networks used by billions of people, which gives the United States a unique ability to shape public debate worldwide.

sections.title: The decline of a contested model

blocks.text: Soft power is a fragile resource: it depends entirely on credibility. In 2003, the invasion of Iraq, launched without the approval of the **UN** and justified by evidence of weapons that proved false, did lasting damage to the image of the United States, seen by some ever since as an imperial power.

Other, internal crises had the same effect: the financial crash of 2008 discredited the American economic model, and the assault on the Capitol in January 2021 weakened the image of the United States as a stable democracy. When a country stops living by its values, its influence collapses.

At the same time, a new form of influence has emerged: the **[[“Brussels Effect”]]**. The European Union sets rules on its own market, on data protection or the environment, so strict that large companies prefer to apply them everywhere rather than adapt country by country. Influence then travels not through dreams but through law.

sections.title: A multipolar world and a battle of stories

blocks.text: The United States is no longer alone on the field of attraction. China invests in cultural institutes and in immense infrastructure projects across Asia and Africa, offering an alternative model of development that appeals to many countries of the Global South.

Other countries bet on a more targeted soft power. Japan charms through manga and food, while South Korea has built its own cultural wave, **[[Hallyu]]** (music, TV series, cinema), which has won a global audience. Cultural appeal is no longer reserved to the West.

An annual ranking called the Soft Power 30 measures how attractive countries are. The United States held first place for years, then slipped behind France and Germany during Donald Trump's presidency, proof of the direct link between foreign policy and a country's image.

American soft power, built on cinema, universities and digital technology, remains the most structuring force of influence in globalization. But it faces more and more competition from new models: China, South Korea and even the European Union.
